What does every official document have in common?

Long image

A

Answer

Every operative official document carries a small structural grammar — identity, origin, date, body, authentication, annex. That grammar is a system-level regularity, not a universal: no stem slot appears in every documented lineage.

  1. Fourteen slots recur across 28 systems on six continents, c. 1412–2024.
  2. Genre, not nation, is the main axis of variation: letters and normative acts fill different slots.
  3. Authentication is the strongest slot: 17 of 25 systems, 13 of 18 lineages.
  4. A registered lineage audit found no stem slot in every lineage, so the atlas regraded the claim in 2026.

Applies to28 systems25 with page slotswritten official documentsatlas v1.4, 2026-10-28

1

What counts as an official document here?

A document is a control record: it reconstitutes an action for a reader who was not present when the action happened. What makes it official is not the paper, the seal or the letterhead but the attribution chain — who may act, by what competence, in what form.1

The boundary is the written document

Two non-documentary record systems bound the claim: the Inka khipu (knotted cord) and Haudenosaunee wampum (shell beads). They carry authority without writing, so the atlas treats them as a boundary rather than as failures of the model.

The corpus is a convenience sample of 28 systems, not a random draw from the world's document regimes. Every claim is conditional on that frame, and the atlas says so wherever it makes one.

2

What are the fourteen slots?

Fourteen functional positions recur. They are not sections of a page: a slot can be carried by layout, by wording, by a stamp, or by a database field.1

Diagram structure
  • Official document root
  • Who and where who
  • When when
  • Who it goes to route
  • What it does act
  • How it is guaranteed close
  • S1 identity s1
  • S2 identifier s2
  • S3 origin s3
  • S4 authority mark s4
  • S5 temporal s5
  • S6 destination s6
  • S7 reference s7
  • S8 subject s8
  • S9 setting s9
  • S10 body s10
  • S11 dispositif s11
  • S12 authentication s12
  • S13 annex s13
  • S14 trace s14
  • root → who
  • root → when
  • root → route
  • root → act
  • root → close
  • who → s1
  • who → s2
  • who → s3
  • who → s4
  • when → s5
  • route → s6
  • route → s7
  • route → s8
  • act → s9
  • act → s10
  • act → s11
  • close → s12
  • close → s13
  • close → s14

The distinction that matters most is inside "what it does". The setting (S9) explains why the act exists; the dispositif (S11) is the operative sentence that orders, grants or prohibits. A document can describe a decision without deciding anything, which is why the two are separate slots.

3

How common is each slot?

  • S12 authentication — 17 of 25
  • S10 body — 14 of 25
  • S1 identity — 11 of 25
  • S2 identifier — 11 of 25
  • S14 trace — 11 of 25
  • S8 subject — 10 of 25
  • S4 authority mark — 9 of 25
  • S7 reference — 9 of 25
  • S13 annex — 9 of 25
  • S3 origin — 8 of 25
  • S5 temporal — 8 of 25
  • S6 destination — 8 of 25
  • S11 dispositif — 4 of 25
  • S9 setting — 2 of 25

No slot is universal even at this level: the best, authentication, reaches 17 of 25. The rarest are the setting (2 systems) and the dispositif (4) — the two slots that make an act normative.1

4

Why do a letter and a law look different?

The stem splits into two declensions by genre. A letter fills the routing slots and drops the preamble; a normative act does the reverse.1

Letter (epistolary)Normative act
Destination (S6)names a recipientFilledEmpty
Reference (S7)FilledOften empty
Setting (S9)Emptyjustifies the actFilled
Dispositif (S11)Rareorders or grantsFilled
ExamplesUA letter, DE DIN 5008, CN 信函格式UN resolution, EU regulation, UA наказ, CN 命令

One joint pattern, not six separate rules

The census fact is that the preamble never co-occurs with authority mark, addressee, reference, subject, body or trace. The registered audit showed that no individual "never" edge is surprising at 25 systems; each becomes informative only at 44–94 systems. The six together, however, reject independence at exact p = 10/300. Under a tradition-blocked null the joint pattern does not reject (p = 1/3 over six placements). Report it as one population-level pattern, not as six laws.2

5

Is the grammar universal?

Not in the strict sense. The registered B3 audit re-derived the six stem slots at lineage level, using a table of documented transmission frozen before any statistic.3

Stem slotSystems (of 25) → lineages (of 18)
S1 identity11 → 8
S3 origin8 → 7
S5 temporal8 → 6
S10 body14 → 11
S12 authentication17 → 13
S13 annex9 → 8
  • 0 of 6 stem slots are present in every lineage, under both the "at least one carrier" and the "every member" reading.3
  • No lineage clustering: p = 0.518, and within-lineage agreement is slightly lower than between-lineage (T = −0.062). Document form does not track the descent lines the atlas documents.
  • Authentication still ranks first at 13 of 18 lineages, but its 95 % interval (0.465–0.903) does not license "most systems".
  • The preamble appears in 2 of 18 lineages, consistent with a genre effect rather than a transmitted template.

So what drives the convergence?

Not descent: there is no detectable lineage clustering. Not a universal: no stem slot survives de-duplication. Genre, function and instrument type remain candidates, and this study cannot separate them. That is the current frontier, stated as an open question rather than a conclusion.

Two properties make the claims checkable rather than rhetorical. First, every claim in the ledger points to a retrieved source, and a gate fails the build if a citation does not resolve. Second, the audits were pre-registered: the hypotheses, nulls and decision rules were committed before the numbers were computed, and departures are logged.1

The regrade in this page is the method working. The atlas previously called the stem "universal"; the lineage audit tested that, failed to support it, and the prose was corrected in version 1.4 rather than defended.

7

What does this not tell you?

  • No standard optimises for efficiency. None claims its format is the most efficient carrier of official information, and the project has not tested that claim.
  • The machine comprehension test is exploratory. It says nothing about how people read formal documents.
  • The corpus is a convenience frame. "The world's documents" is a working scope, not a sample.
  • One system is provisional. The Russian ГОСТ case rests on blocked primary hosts and is labelled as a placeholder.
  • The sources are not redistributed here. The public repository omits third-party texts; the ledger keeps their URLs.

Do not quote 17 of 25 as a majority

The 95 % interval for authentication at system level is 0.465–0.851. The count may be quoted; "most systems" may not, because the lower bound falls below one half.3

8

Try it: read a document in six passes

Diagram structure
  • Who issued it issuer
  • When and where when
  • Who it is for to
  • What it does act
  • Who guarantees it auth
  • Where it has been trace
  • act → auth
  • auth → trace
  • issuer → when
  • to → act
  • when → to

Take any official letter, order or certificate you can legally inspect. Work through the passes, and write down what carries each one — a position on the page, a phrase, a stamp, a field.

  1. Who issued it ↗

    Read the letterhead or signature block. Name the office, not just the person; competence is the point.

  2. When and where ↗

    Separate the date of the act from the date of receipt or registration. They can sit in different slots.

  3. Who it is for ↗

    A named addressee signals a letter. A general address signals an act that binds whoever it reaches.

  4. What it does ↗

    Find the operative verb: orders, grants, prohibits, records. If you cannot find one, the document may only describe.

  5. Who guarantees it ↗

    Signature, seal, register entry, cryptographic signature: ask which person or office the mark binds.

  6. Where it has been ↗

    Registration numbers, stamps, filing marks. The trace is often the only evidence the document entered a system.
